Diagnosis: Over-specification (users copying A100-80 GB templates for 35 GB memory jobs), pool fragmentation, and legacy V100 avoidance leave A100-40 GB and V100 nodes idle while large jobs wait for A100-80 GB allocations. The scheduler correctly enforced policies written for a homogeneous fleet that no longer matched the heterogeneous infrastructure.
Systems lesson: Surface-level diagnosis often mistakes policy-infrastructure mismatches for scheduling algorithm bugs. Updating distribution layer policies to support automatic capability matching, dynamic memory profiling, and backfilling raises cluster utilization to 84 percent, recovering $7M in annual compute capacity.





Table 9: Utilization recovery results: The distinction between “allocated” and “effective” utilization captures the policy-induced utilization gap: before the fix, A100-80 GB GPUs showed high allocation in Slurm but lower actual compute utilization, while strict job templates stranded other capable hardware pools. This utilization gain adds approximately 246 fully utilized GPUs of productive work (table 9). That is equivalent to buying 410 additional raw GPUs if those GPUs ran at the old 60 percent utilization. At $2/GPU-hour, the equivalent raw capacity represents approximately $7M in annual recovered value, achieved through policy changes requiring zero additional hardware investment.

Common utilization anti-patterns
High-level metrics often mask deep inefficiencies. A cluster dashboard may report 85 percent allocation, but productive utilization, the share of cycles actually advancing model state, can be significantly lower. Debugging these gaps requires identifying specific signatures in the GPU telemetry that reveal the underlying bottleneck.
The zombie job represents the most egregious waste: a training process that has crashed or deadlocked but continues to hold GPU resources. In a distributed run training a 175B parameter model, a single rank failure can leave 128 GPUs allocated but idling if the process cleanup fails. The signature is high memory allocation (greater than 300 GB) paired with near-zero SM utilization (less than 5 percent) persisting for longer than a heartbeat timeout (typically 10 minutes). This state often results from CUDA context corruption or a driver-level deadlock that prevents the container runtime from successfully reaping the process, requiring forceful node-level remediation to reclaim the device.
The data starvation pattern manifests as a high-frequency sawtooth wave in GPU utilization, where the device oscillates between 100 percent load (forward/backward pass) and 0 percent load (waiting for the next batch). While the average utilization might appear acceptable at 60 to 70 percent, the GPU is effectively idling for a third of its life. This occurs when the CPU-bound data pipeline cannot sustain the throughput required by the GPU, a common scenario in computer vision where JPEG decoding and augmentation saturate host CPUs. A utilization variance exceeding 30 percent standard deviation is the primary diagnostic indicator, signaling the need for active prefetching, increased loader parallelism, or local NVMe caching to saturate the accelerator.
The communication bottleneck reveals itself through periodic, synchronized drops in SM utilization across all ranks in a distributed group. For the 175B model, synchronizing gradients for 350 GB of parameters requires massive bandwidth; if the network is undersized or congested, the GPUs spend more time waiting for AllReduce to complete than performing computation. The diagnostic metric is the step time ratio. If total iteration time exceeds 1.5\(\times\) compute-only time (forward plus backward passes in isolation), non-compute overhead exceeds 0.5\(\times\) compute time, which is material but not dominant. Under the simplified decomposition \(T_{\text{total}} = T_{\text{compute}} + T_{\text{comm}}\), communication exceeds computation only when the ratio is greater than 2\(\times\); profiling must also separate communication from input and runtime overhead. Remediation requires topology-aware placement to keep traffic on high-bandwidth switch tiers or algorithmic changes like gradient accumulation to increase the compute-to-communication ratio.
The memory fragmentation trap is an insidious failure mode in long-running inference servers. A 175B model serving diverse request lengths can end up with 80 percent of its HBM allocated to the KV cache, yet be unable to accept a new request because the free memory is scattered in small, noncontiguous blocks. The GPU appears full to the scheduler but underutilized in terms of throughput. This resembles the classic heap fragmentation problem but with higher stakes: a single restart to defragment dumps hundreds of gigabytes of state. Monitoring the ratio of requested token slots to allocated memory bytes often exposes this gap, which paged cache allocators address by decoupling logical sequence contiguity from physical memory layout, recovering usable memory and boosting serving throughput by 2–4\(\times\) without adding hardware.
The debugging example illustrates a broader principle that applies to every system across the fleet stack: scheduling systems are only as effective as the policies they implement, and policies must evolve alongside infrastructure. When infrastructure changes (new hardware generations are added, network topologies are upgraded, workload mixes shift from training-dominant to serving-dominant), the policies encoded in scheduler configuration, job templates, and organizational practices must be re-evaluated and updated. The most expensive scheduling bug is often not a software defect but a policy that was correct for the old infrastructure and was never updated for the new one.
This principle connects scheduling mechanics to fleet governance. Technical policies (GPU type matching, gang scheduling timeouts, preemption grace periods) interact with organizational policies (team quotas, priority hierarchies, cost allocation) and human behavior (job template reuse, resource request habits, queue submission patterns). Effective fleet orchestration requires attending to all three layers simultaneously.

Self-Check: Question

An administrator observes that average GPU compute utilization across a 1,000-GPU cluster is only \(55\%\), yet users experience multi-day queue wait times for 64-GPU jobs. Which diagnostic finding points to the primary root cause?

The cluster’s Ethernet cables are physically too long, causing optical signals to decay into radio waves.
Severe resource fragmentation and strict gang scheduling constraints prevent 64-GPU contiguous blocks from forming, while short jobs hold scattered GPUs across nodes without filling them.
The NVIDIA driver automatically caps utilization at 55% when GPU fans are running on low speed.
Python code running in user containers automatically halts execution whenever cluster utilization drops below 60%.

During a multi-GPU training job, DCGM reports that GPU SM utilization oscillates rapidly between \(10\%\) and \(95\%\) with low memory copy throughput, while top on the host node shows \(100\%\) CPU utilization across all cores and high disk wait (\(iowait\)). What is the root cause and remedy?

The GPU hardware is defective; the operator should replace the GPUs with CPU-only nodes.
The PyTorch model has too many layers; the model architecture must be pruned to 1 layer.
The training job is bottlenecked on host data loading, decompression, or augmentation; the remedy is optimizing PyTorch num_workers, utilizing shared memory (/dev/shm), caching preprocessed tensors on local NVMe SSDs, or offloading transforms to GPU using DALI.
The cluster InfiniBand switch is operating in half-duplex mode; the administrator must power cycle the spine switch.

What is a ‘zombie allocation’ (or ghost job) in a GPU cluster, and how can automated health monitors detect and remediate it?
True or False: In a ring AllReduce across 32 nodes, if 31 nodes show \(95\%\) GPU utilization and 1 node shows \(10\%\) utilization, the node with \(10\%\) utilization is the only healthy node while the 31 nodes are encountering network hardware faults.
When diagnosing training performance bottlenecks, operators inspect the ____ throughput (measured in GB/s) to ensure that batches transferred from host memory to accelerator HBM are not constrained by host bus contention.

title: The Scheduling Problem
text:
Fallacies and Pitfalls
Those policy-infrastructure mismatches recur as a small set of misconceptions that can make an apparently healthy scheduler waste expensive fleet capacity. It is tempting to look at a cluster running at 98 percent utilization and declare victory, only to discover that researchers have stopped submitting jobs entirely because wait times have stretched into weeks. Cluster orchestration is riddled with counterintuitive traps like this, where optimizing a single metric destroys overall system value.

Fallacy: More sophisticated scheduling algorithms always improve utilization.
Engineers facing low utilization often reach for more advanced schedulers, assuming the algorithm is the bottleneck. As the debugging example in section 1.8 demonstrates, the root cause is frequently policy misconfiguration, not algorithmic limitation. A simple FIFO scheduler with correct policies (capability-based matching, backfill with timeouts, appropriate gang scheduling constraints) often outperforms a sophisticated scheduler with incorrect policies. Before upgrading the scheduler, audit the policies: confirm that users are not requesting resources they do not need, that heterogeneous resources are properly exposed, and that gang-scheduling timeouts are configured.


Pitfall: Treating all GPU-hours as equal when measuring utilization.
Cluster dashboards commonly report “GPU utilization” as a single percentage, averaging across all GPUs and all workloads. This metric hides critical information. A cluster might report 80 percent utilization where 60 percent is productive training, 15 percent is idle GPUs allocated to jobs waiting for gang completion, and 5 percent is GPUs running data loading with no active computation. Effective monitoring distinguishes between allocated utilization (GPUs assigned to jobs), compute utilization (GPUs executing kernels), and productive utilization (GPUs advancing useful training or serving requests). Only the last metric correlates with actual value delivered.


Fallacy: Gang scheduling is always necessary for distributed training.
Gang scheduling prevents deadlock for synchronous training, but not all distributed training is synchronous. Asynchronous training methods tolerate worker arrivals and departures, and elastic training frameworks handle variable worker counts. For workloads that can operate asynchronously or elastically, relaxing the gang scheduling requirement dramatically improves scheduling flexibility and reduces queue wait times. The trade-off is potential convergence degradation from stale gradients or batch size variability, but for many practical workloads (hyperparameter sweeps, fine-tuning, pretraining with adaptive batch size), this trade-off is favorable.


Pitfall: Setting static quotas based on peak demand.
Organizations commonly set team quotas to handle worst-case demand, reasoning that teams need guaranteed access during crunch periods. If Team A’s peak demand is 500 GPUs and Team B’s is 300 GPUs, the cluster needs 800 GPUs with static quotas. In practice, peaks rarely coincide. Hierarchical fair-share with borrowing can serve both teams’ peak demands with a 600-GPU cluster, because when Team A peaks, Team B is typically at moderate demand and can yield borrowed capacity. Static quotas at peak levels waste 25 to 40 percent of cluster capacity on guaranteed-but-unused allocations.


Fallacy: Spot instances are always cheaper for training.
The 60 to 90 percent discount on spot instances creates the impression of automatic savings. The effective cost depends on interruption frequency, checkpoint overhead, and restart time. For a large model with 15-minute checkpoint times and 30-minute restart times, a spot interruption costs 45 minutes of productive time. If interruptions occur every 2 hours, the effective cost rises enough that the nominal 65 percent discount shrinks to about 52 percent savings. For 100B+ parameter models with slow checkpointing on clusters with frequent spot interruptions, on-demand instances can actually be cheaper when accounting for all overhead. The decision requires quantitative analysis of the specific workload and spot market conditions, not blanket assumptions about cost savings.


Pitfall: Ignoring topology when scheduling distributed training.
Schedulers that treat GPUs as interchangeable units create allocations where tensor parallel groups span nodes (forcing NVLink-speed operations over InfiniBand) or AllReduce groups cross spine switches (adding latency and congestion). The 15 to 30 percent throughput penalty from poor topology placement accumulates over multi-week training runs, potentially wasting more resources than would be lost by waiting for a topology-aware allocation. Topology-aware scheduling increases scheduling complexity and may reduce packing efficiency, but for large distributed training jobs, the throughput improvement often justifies the trade-off.


Fallacy: GPU utilization alone is a sufficient autoscaling signal.
GPU utilization is a poor proxy for inference health. A GPU can be 90 percent utilized but still violating latency SLOs because the utilization comes from processing a backlog of queued requests. Conversely, a GPU at 40 percent utilization might be perfectly healthy if it is serving low-latency requests with headroom for bursts. The right metrics are queue depth, P99 latency relative to SLO, and KV cache memory pressure for LLM workloads. Relying on utilization creates a lagging indicator that only triggers scaling after performance has already degraded, whereas queue depth and SLO margin provide leading indicators that allow the fleet to scale before the user experience suffers. Furthermore, for LLMs, memory exhaustion from KV cache growth can occur at low compute utilization, causing requests to stall or fail. An autoscaler watching only compute utilization will miss this failure mode entirely, leaving the service degraded despite apparent capacity.


Pitfall: Using elastic training to avoid gang-scheduling decisions.
Elastic training complements but does not replace gang scheduling. While it allows jobs to resize, the resizing steps themselves often have atomic requirements. Elastic training works for data parallelism but not tensor parallelism (which requires a fixed number of GPUs per group). A 175B model using 8-way tensor parallelism needs exactly 8 GPUs per tensor-parallel group to function; this is a gang constraint that elastic training cannot relax. Elastic training adjusts the number of data-parallel replicas, not the intra-replica parallelism configuration, meaning the scheduler must still enforce gang constraints for the base unit of the model. If a scheduler naively places these 8 GPUs across different racks or fails to allocate them atomically, the tensor parallel group will either fail to initialize or suffer catastrophic performance degradation.


Fallacy: The scheduler needs no workload-specific validation.
Scheduler configuration requires continuous tuning as workloads evolve. Default configurations in Slurm or Kubernetes are optimized for generic workloads, often prioritizing simple fairness over throughput. ML-specific tuning (gang scheduling timeouts, topology-aware placement weights, preemption grace periods, and fair-share decay rates) can improve utilization by 15 to 25 percent. Organizations that deploy a scheduler and never revisit its configuration leave significant value on the table. A default preemption grace period might be too short for a large model to checkpoint, causing wasted work, while an untuned topology weight might fragment the cluster unnecessarily. As the cluster grows and the workload mix shifts (for example, from training-heavy to inference-heavy), the effective scheduling parameters shift with it. Treating the scheduler as a set-and-forget appliance lets the fleet drift into inefficiency.


Pitfall: Treating high utilization as proof of cluster health.
A cluster running at 95 percent utilization sounds efficient but may indicate a problem: insufficient capacity that is choking experimentation velocity. When utilization consistently exceeds 85 to 90 percent, queue times grow rapidly following the well-known M/M/1 queuing result from stochastic process theory. In this model, average wait time is proportional to \(\rho/(1-\rho)\) where \(\rho\) is utilization; at 90 percent utilization, average wait is 9\(\times\) the service time, and at 95 percent, it is 19\(\times\). Researchers waiting hours or days for resources conduct fewer experiments, test fewer hypotheses, and iterate more slowly on model designs. This reduced experimentation velocity has real costs that are harder to quantify than GPU-hours but may be larger in aggregate. The effective utilization target balances resource efficiency against researcher productivity, often landing between 70 and 85 percent for training clusters where queue responsiveness directly affects research output. Inference clusters, where requests are served immediately or not at all, often target even lower utilization (50 to 70 percent) to maintain latency headroom for traffic spikes.
Recognizing these fallacies prevents platform teams from chasing false optimizations that look good on dashboards but degrade developer velocity. The core orchestration principles that successfully navigate these trade-offs share a common thread: they treat scheduling as an engineering discipline, not an administrative function.


Self-Check: Question

Why is targeting near \(100\%\) GPU cluster utilization an operational anti-pattern for an interactive AI research and development organization?

GPU hardware components melt if utilization exceeds \(90\%\) for more than 5 consecutive minutes.
Modern deep learning frameworks automatically downgrade model accuracy when cluster utilization exceeds \(85\%\).
Operating above \(95\%\) utilization causes cloud providers to double their hourly billing rates without warning.
As utilization approaches \(100\%\), queuing theory (Pollaczek-Khinchine) dictates that job queue wait times explode hyperbolically, delaying fast feedback for exploratory experiments and severely reducing overall engineering velocity.

Explain the fallacy that ‘more sophisticated scheduling algorithms always improve utilization,’ and describe what operators should audit before replacing their cluster scheduler.
True or False: Gang scheduling is strictly mandatory for every distributed ML workload, including asynchronous parameter-server training, hyperparameter sweeps, and elastic fine-tuning jobs.

See Answers →

title: The Scheduling Problem
text:
Summary
Fleet orchestration transforms raw data center capacity into productive ML infrastructure by governing how silicon, bandwidth, and state interact across time and space. In terms of the iron law of performance (\(T \approx D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW} + O/(R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}}) + L_{\text{lat}}\)), the orchestrator is the system’s central optimizer: placement strategies preserve fabric bandwidth (\(\text{BW}\)), multi-tenancy and quota policies drive realized hardware efficiency (\(\eta_{\text{hw}}\)), and distributed scheduling algorithms bound queue delay and coordination overhead (\(L_{\text{lat}}\)). The difference between a high-performing cluster and thousands of idle accelerators is not hardware capability, but the scheduler’s ability to navigate the trade-offs between atomic consistency, fault tolerance, and placement topology under partial failures and bursty demand.
The chapter’s unifying technical insight is that placement directly dictates physical performance. By aligning model parallelism with the physical network hierarchy, topology-aware scheduling prevents cross-rack bisection bottlenecks, protecting the \(D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW}\) communication term and increasing throughput by 15 to 30 percent. Domain-specific schedulers—such as Tiresias, Gandiva, Themis, and Pollux—exploit the structure of ML workloads (iterative progress, heavy-tailed runtimes, and predictable convergence scaling) to minimize the coordination and wait-time terms (\(L_{\text{lat}}\)), cutting average job completion time by 40 to 60 percent compared to general-purpose FIFO policies. Elastic training and spot management extend this control by trading worker continuity for economic flexibility, provided jobs can dynamically adapt without incurring unacceptable preemption tax.
At serving time, the scheduling objective shifts from throughput maximization to tail-latency protection. Serving fleets cannot trade queue wait for utilization; autoscaling must respond to leading indicators—queue depth, P99 latency margin, and KV-cache memory pressure—rather than compute utilization alone, which misses memory-bound stalls. Meanwhile, multi-tenant isolation mechanisms (MIG, MPS, time-slicing) and fair-share quota governance prevent noisy-neighbor interference and quota hoarding, ensuring that high aggregate allocation translates directly into high effective hardware efficiency (\(\eta_{\text{hw}}\)).
Ultimately, fleet orchestration is diagnostic and economic as much as algorithmic. Operational pathologies such as zombie jobs, data starvation, topology mismatch, and pool fragmentation are symptoms of policy-infrastructure misalignment rather than deficient hardware. When compute nodes are defined, networks wired, storage attached, fault tolerance integrated, and orchestrators aligned, the fleet transitions from a collection of isolated servers into a coherent, self-healing computing platform.

Key Takeaways: Scheduling is systems engineering

Distributed scheduling is fundamentally hard: Cluster scheduling faces challenges (partial failures, network partitions, state inconsistency) that single-machine schedulers never encounter. The CAP theorem forces trade-offs between consistency and availability that shape every scheduling system’s design.
Gang scheduling prevents deadlock but reduces flexibility: Gang scheduling gives distributed training atomic resource allocation to prevent hold-and-wait deadlocks, but rigid gang scheduling wastes resources when combined with backfill timeouts and elastic training alternatives.
Topology determines performance: Where GPUs are placed within the cluster hierarchy matters as much as how many GPUs a job receives. NVLink vs. InfiniBand placement decisions can create 15 to 30 percent throughput differences for the same job on the same hardware.
ML-specific scheduling outperforms generic approaches: Exploiting workload characteristics (predictable resource needs, iterative computation, diminishing returns) enables 40 to 60 percent improvements in job completion time compared to general-purpose FIFO or fair-share policies.
Utilization is a first-order economic driver: Improving cluster utilization from 50 percent to 80 percent on a large cluster effectively adds thousands of GPUs worth of capacity. Closing this gap through policy and algorithm work pays back faster than buying additional accelerators.
Policies must evolve with infrastructure: Scheduling algorithms are only as effective as the policies they implement. When infrastructure changes (heterogeneous hardware additions, topology upgrades, workload mix shifts), policies must be re-evaluated and updated (principle \(\ref{pri-conservation-overhead}\)).



The fleet now has compute, communication, storage, and the resilience to keep them running. It still needs a policy that decides what runs where. A scheduler that chases peak utilization can deadlock when large jobs compete for the same nodes, while a scheduler that guarantees progress may leave some capacity deliberately unused. The gap between theoretical and safely sustainable throughput is the price of coordination. At fleet scale, performance therefore depends not only on hardware speed but also on the policy that allocates it.

What’s Next: From orchestration to optimizationWith distributed execution established in Distributed Training and fault-tolerant checkpointing in Fault Tolerance, multi-tenant resource management completes the operational foundation of the machine learning fleet. With the orchestrator placing workloads on the right hardware tiers, the next challenge is maximizing single-node and intra-step efficiency. Performance Engineering examines operator fusion, precision engineering, graph compilation, and execution scheduling. Orchestration allocates the right resources; performance engineering extracts peak throughput from them.




Self-Check: Question

Which statement best synthesizes the central architectural challenge of fleet orchestration for machine learning?

Orchestration is purely a software compilation task that translates PyTorch code into C++ CUDA binaries without considering cluster hardware.
Orchestration requires balancing physical hardware constraints (NVLink topology, failure rates, power limits) against organizational policies (fairness, priorities, cost) across diverse, long-running, and failure-prone distributed workloads.
Orchestration has been completely solved by standard web application load balancers like NGINX, which handle GPU AllReduce synchronization transparently.
Orchestration only matters for single-GPU laptops and has no relevance to multi-thousand GPU datacenters.

How is the historical boundary between HPC batch scheduling (Slurm) and cloud-native service orchestration (Kubernetes) evolving to meet the demands of modern ML lifecycles?
True or False: In large-scale ML cluster management, maximizing raw GPU allocated utilization (the percentage of GPUs assigned to active containers) guarantees optimal economic value and research productivity.

title: The Scheduling Problem
text:
Self-Check Answers

Self-Check: Answer

What is the fundamental difference in control philosophy between Slurm and Kubernetes when managing distributed ML training workloads?

Slurm relies on continuous reconciliation loops against desired state stored in etcd, whereas Kubernetes executes imperative one-time allocation scripts via a centralized daemon.
Slurm uses peer-to-peer gossip protocols to schedule tasks across nodes, whereas Kubernetes enforces hierarchical master-slave token ring passing.
Slurm employs an imperative allocation model where users request explicit physical resources guaranteed at launch, whereas Kubernetes uses a declarative model where controllers continuously reconcile observed cluster state toward declared desired state.
Slurm schedules containerized microservices with dynamic horizontal auto-scaling, whereas Kubernetes only supports uncontainerized bare-metal MPI processes.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Slurm originates from HPC batch systems and uses an imperative model (sbatch requests explicit resources like --gres=gpu:8 --nodes=4), providing authoritative upfront allocation. Kubernetes uses a declarative model where controllers continuously observe actual state and execute reconciliation loops to converge toward desired state (e.g., Pods, Deployments). The option swapping Slurm and Kubernetes mechanisms reverses their core architectures. The gossip protocol alternative invents a non-existent scheduling model for Slurm. The containerization claim reverses the platforms’ primary native workload types.
Learning Objective: Compare the core architectural control mechanisms of Slurm and Kubernetes for ML training workflows.
How does NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitioning on A100/H100 accelerators differ from software-based GPU time-slicing in multi-tenant serving environments?

MIG uses OS-level software schedulers to alternate kernel execution times, but shares the same L2 cache and memory controllers dynamically.
MIG compiles user PyTorch models into specialized FPGA bitstreams, preventing simultaneous execution of untrusted kernels.
MIG allows dynamic resizing of GPU partitions on a millisecond basis without draining running containers or resetting the device.
MIG partitions the physical accelerator into hardware-isolated instances with dedicated streaming multiprocessors (SMs), memory controllers, and L2 cache slices, eliminating noisy-neighbor interference at the cost of static partition reconfiguration.

Answer: The correct answer is D. MIG provides true hardware-level partitioning (up to 7 instances on A100/H100) with dedicated SMs, memory controllers, and private L2 cache slices, preventing memory bus contention and noisy-neighbor performance degradation. Its primary trade-off is reconfiguration rigidity: changing MIG profile configurations requires draining all active workloads on the physical GPU. The software-scheduling description applies to standard time-slicing or MPS rather than MIG. The FPGA compilation claim is factually false. The millisecond dynamic resizing contradicts MIG’s static partitioning constraints.
Learning Objective: Evaluate Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) architectural characteristics and trade-offs for multi-tenant inference.
In Slurm’s fair-share priority formula (\(\text{Priority}_{\text{effective}} = \text{Priority}_{\text{base}} \times \frac{F_{\text{target}}}{F_{\text{actual}} + \epsilon}\)), what role does the usage decay half-life play, and what is the trade-off between setting a short versus a long half-life?
Answer: The half-life determines how quickly the scheduler discounts past GPU consumption in \(F_{\text{actual}}\), allowing heavy users to gradually restore their priority. A short half-life (e.g., 1-2 days) rapidly restores priority but can cause oscillatory usage where teams cycle between hogging and starvation; a long half-life (e.g., 2-4 weeks) stabilizes priority order but penalizes researchers long after a major burst project has completed.
Learning Objective: Explain the mechanics and purpose of usage half-life decay in Slurm’s fair-share scheduling formula.
Why do high-performance distributed training jobs in Kubernetes typically enable hostNetwork: true and leverage the NVIDIA Network Operator instead of relying on default Container Network Interface (CNI) overlay networks?
Answer: Standard CNI overlay networks (such as VXLAN or Calico) introduce packet encapsulation overhead, CPU switching latency, and lack direct integration with hardware RDMA subsystems. Enabling hostNetwork: true allows worker pods to bypass container network namespaces, enabling direct access to host InfiniBand/RoCE network adapters and GPUDirect RDMA for full-bandwidth, sub-microsecond AllReduce collective communication.
Learning Objective: Justify why large-scale distributed training jobs in Kubernetes require host networking rather than standard container overlay networks.
True or False: Kueue replaces the native Kubernetes kube-scheduler binary entirely to implement custom gang scheduling algorithms, whereas Volcano acts purely as an admission controller layered on top of the default scheduler.
Answer: False. The roles are reversed: Volcano is an alternative scheduler that replaces kube-scheduler to provide native PodGroup-based gang scheduling, whereas Kueue is an admission controller that manages when jobs enter the cluster (using ClusterQueues and borrowing) while delegating actual pod placement to the default kube-scheduler or specialized placement plugins.
Learning Objective: Differentiate between scheduler replacement (Volcano) and queue admission control (Kueue) in the Kubernetes batch ecosystem.
**Order the following steps in the lifecycle of a distributed training job submitted to a Kubernetes cluster configured with Kubeflow Training Operator and Volcano gang scheduling:


The PodGroup is created and Volcano verifies that the cluster can simultaneously satisfy the minimum worker requirement (\(N_{\text{min}}\)).
The developer submits a PyTorchJob custom resource manifest defining worker replicas, GPU limits, and rendezvous parameters.
Volcano binds all worker pods to specific healthy nodes simultaneously, and kubelets start the training containers with GPUDirect RDMA.
Workers establish distributed communication via TorchElastic rendezvous (setting MASTER_ADDR and WORLD_SIZE) and begin synchronized training steps.
The Kubeflow Training Operator reconciles the PyTorchJob, creating the individual worker pods and a corresponding Volcano PodGroup.**

Answer: The correct order is (2) -> (5) -> (1) -> (3) -> (4). Explanation: Step (2): The developer submits a PyTorchJob custom resource manifest defining worker replicas, GPU limits, and rendezvous parameters. Step (5): The Kubeflow Training Operator reconciles the PyTorchJob, creating the individual worker pods and a corresponding Volcano PodGroup. Step (1): The PodGroup is created and Volcano verifies that the cluster can simultaneously satisfy the minimum worker requirement (\(N_{\text{min}}\)). Step (3): Volcano binds all worker pods to specific healthy nodes simultaneously, and kubelets start the training containers with GPUDirect RDMA. Step (4): Workers establish distributed communication via TorchElastic rendezvous (setting MASTER_ADDR and WORLD_SIZE) and begin synchronized training steps.
Learning Objective: Order the operational stages of launching a distributed PyTorch training job via the Kubeflow Training Operator and Volcano.
← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

When scheduling a 3D-parallel large language model across a multi-rack GPU cluster, how should Tensor Parallelism (TP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), and Data Parallelism (DP) be mapped across the topology hierarchy to maximize throughput?

Map DP strictly within intra-node NVLink domains, TP across inter-rack spine switches, and PP across rail-aligned network switches.
Map PP strictly within intra-node NVLink domains, DP across Top-of-Rack switches, and TP across multi-hop spine switches.
Map TP strictly within intra-node NVLink domains (highest bandwidth), PP within the same rack or adjacent switches (point-to-point activations), and DP across nodes with rail-aligned network switches.
Map TP, PP, and DP uniformly at random across all available nodes to balance switch thermal loads across the datacenter fabric.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Tensor Parallelism requires frequent, high-volume AllReduce collectives at every transformer layer, necessitating the extreme bandwidth of intra-node NVLink (450-900 GB/s per direction). Pipeline Parallelism transfers point-to-point activations between adjacent pipeline stages, fitting well within intra-rack or adjacent leaf switches. Data Parallelism performs gradient AllReduce once per step, which can be overlapped with backward compute and optimized across nodes using rail-aligned InfiniBand/RoCE fabrics. Reversing TP and DP places massive layer-by-layer collectives over slow inter-rack links, causing severe throughput collapse. Uniform random mapping ignores bandwidth cliffs and causes massive cross-spine contention.
Learning Objective: Design an optimal mapping of 3D parallelism dimensions (Tensor, Pipeline, Data) onto a multi-tier cluster topology hierarchy.
In a multi-node cluster where binary up/down health probes report all switches healthy but an AllReduce collective experiences a \(30\%\) throughput degradation due to high CRC error rates on a single leaf switch, what is the optimal orchestration response?

Continue running the job indefinitely because a 10-minute checkpoint-and-reschedule migration would cost more compute than a 30% slowdown over a multi-week run.
Rely on the GPU driver to disable NVLink and route all tensor-parallel traffic through host memory over PCIe.
Trigger a performance-aware topology quarantine via taints or drain states, checkpoint the running job, and migrate it to healthy nodes where the break-even time is under an hour.
Terminate the job and permanently de-allocate all 10,000 GPUs in the datacenter until all network transceivers are manually replaced.

Answer: The correct answer is C. When a ‘limping switch’ introduces high CRC error rates or packet drops, binary health checks pass while collective performance drops sharply. For multi-day or multi-week training runs, taking a 5 to 15 minute pause to checkpoint, drain/taint the degraded switch path, and migrate to healthy topology breaks even in less than an hour against a 20-30% continuous throughput penalty. Ignoring the issue wastes millions of dollars in idle GPU cycles. Disabling NVLink exacerbates the slowdown. De-allocating the entire datacenter is an extreme operational overreaction.
Learning Objective: Evaluate scheduler diagnostic mechanisms and migration economics for degraded network hardware.
In an 8-GPU-per-node cluster with 8 independent network fabric rails, how does rail-aware scheduling place data-parallel ranks, and why does this prevent network switch congestion?
Answer: Rail-aware scheduling assigns data-parallel rank \(r\) to GPU \(r \bmod 8\) across selected nodes, ensuring that corresponding GPUs communicate strictly over their dedicated, independent network rail switch hierarchy. This isolates each data-parallel collective to a single rail fabric, eliminating cross-rail traffic and switch port contention between parallel communication streams.
Learning Objective: Explain how rail-optimized scheduling eliminates network congestion during multi-node AllReduce collectives.
Why are static topology configuration files (such as Slurm’s topology.conf or static Kubernetes node labels) insufficient on their own for optimal collective placement in large-scale ML clusters?
Answer: Static files represent nominal design schematics rather than operational reality; they cannot reflect dynamic runtime anomalies such as degraded transceiver link widths, PCIe bus renegotiations, blown spine switch links, or thermal throttling. Collective libraries and orchestrators need dynamic runtime introspection (e.g., inspecting /sys/class/infiniband and NCCL telemetry) to map the ground-truth operational fabric and avoid placing sensitive collectives across degraded links.
Learning Objective: Compare static topology configuration files with dynamic runtime topology introspection in distributed ML orchestration.
**Order the steps executed by a topology-aware scheduler when placing a multi-node distributed training job across a multi-tier datacenter fabric:


Filter out candidate nodes that have active taints, hardware ECC alerts, or degraded network link flags.
Allocate contiguous GPU ranks within each node to satisfy intra-node NVLink requirements for Tensor Parallel groups.
Group nodes into the smallest common network domain (such as a single leaf switch or rack) to minimize switch hops for Pipeline Parallel stages.
Receive job submission specifying total GPU count, node granularity, and parallelism dimensions (\(TP, PP, DP\)).
Assign Data Parallel ranks to matching GPU rail indices across nodes to ensure non-interfering AllReduce traffic.**

Answer: The correct order is (4) -> (1) -> (3) -> (2) -> (5). Explanation: Step (4): Receive job submission specifying total GPU count, node granularity, and parallelism dimensions (\(TP, PP, DP\)). Step (1): Filter out candidate nodes that have active taints, hardware ECC alerts, or degraded network link flags. Step (3): Group nodes into the smallest common network domain (such as a single leaf switch or rack) to minimize switch hops for Pipeline Parallel stages. Step (2): Allocate contiguous GPU ranks within each node to satisfy intra-node NVLink requirements for Tensor Parallel groups. Step (5): Assign Data Parallel ranks to matching GPU rail indices across nodes to ensure non-interfering AllReduce traffic.
Learning Objective: Order the decision hierarchy used by a topology-aware scheduler to place a multi-node 3D-parallel training job.

In cloud orchestration environments such as AWS and GCP, a user specifies a ____ to ensure that allocated virtual machine instances are placed within a single high-bandwidth, low-latency network spine domain rather than scattered across the datacenter.
Answer: placement group (or Placement Group, cluster placement group). A placement group acts as the topology contract ensuring that distributed instances share maximum bisection bandwidth for collective AllReduce operations.
Learning Objective: Identify the cloud-native abstraction used to enforce low-latency, high-bandwidth network proximity.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

When an elastic scheduler resizes a distributed training job from 64 GPUs to 128 GPUs, what trade-off exists between maintaining a constant global batch size versus scaling batch size proportionally with worker count?

Constant global batch size preserves mathematical convergence dynamics but halves per-GPU micro-batch size (potentially lowering hardware compute efficiency or hitting memory limits when shrinking), whereas proportional scaling maintains compute efficiency per GPU but alters optimization trajectory and requires learning rate recalibration.
Constant global batch size requires restarting the model weights from epoch zero, whereas proportional batch size allows continuous gradient descent without learning rate adjustment.
Constant global batch size disables NVLink communication across workers, whereas proportional batch size enables ring AllReduce.
Constant global batch size doubles the learning rate automatically via PyTorch hooks, whereas proportional batch size keeps the learning rate fixed to prevent divergence.

Answer: The correct answer is A. In elastic training, if global batch size is kept constant (\(B_{\text{global}} = B_{\text{per-worker}} \times N\)), adding workers reduces \(B_{\text{per-worker}}\), which preserves optimization convergence but may reduce GPU compute utilization (or cause OOM when worker count shrinks and \(B_{\text{per-worker}}\) increases). If per-worker batch size is fixed, scaling \(N\) scales \(B_{\text{global}}\), maintaining per-GPU compute intensity but requiring learning rate recalibration (e.g., linear or square-root scaling) to avoid convergence degradation. The other choices present incorrect claims about restarting weights, NVLink, or inverted learning rate rules.
Learning Objective: Analyze the trade-offs between constant global batch size and adaptive learning rate during elastic worker scaling.
An elastic job running on 64 GPUs at 100 steps/minute can scale to 128 GPUs, reaching 180 steps/minute. If resizing triggers a dynamic rendezvous and checkpoint-sync transition pause of 60 seconds (0 steps during pause), what is the minimum duration the job must remain at 128 GPUs to achieve a net gain in total steps completed?

At least 15 seconds.
At least 30 seconds.
At least 45 seconds.
At least 75 seconds.

Answer: The correct answer is D. In the 60-second (1.0 minute) pause, the 64-GPU baseline would have completed \(100 \text{ steps/min} \times 1.0 \text{ min} = 100 \text{ steps}\). At 128 GPUs, the job produces \(180 \text{ steps/min}\), which is an incremental gain of \(\Delta = 180 - 100 = 80 \text{ steps/min}\). To recover the 100 lost steps, the job must run at 128 GPUs for \(t = 100 / 80 = 1.25 \text{ minutes} = 75 \text{ seconds}\). The choices for 15, 30, and 45 seconds fall well short of recovering the 100 lost steps.
Learning Objective: Calculate the break-even duration required for an elastic scaling resize to deliver positive net training throughput.
What three parameters define the operational contract between an elastic scheduler and an elastic training framework (such as TorchElastic), and why is each necessary?
Answer: The contract is defined by: (1) Elastic Range \([N_{\text{min}}, N_{\text{max}}]\), specifying the valid worker bounds within which the model can train without OOM or synchronization collapse; (2) Transition Cost, the time required for dynamic rendezvous and state reload, bounding the minimum viable resize interval; and (3) Scaling Efficiency Curve, describing throughput gained per added accelerator to let the scheduler determine whether assigning marginal GPUs is more productive than allocating them elsewhere.
Learning Objective: Explain the three core parameters of the contract between an elastic scheduler and a training framework.
True or False: When high-priority workloads surge on a shared cluster, an elastic scheduler can reclaim capacity from lower-priority distributed training jobs by downsizing them toward their \(N_{\text{min}}\) worker limit rather than terminating and requeuing them, thereby avoiding total progress loss.
Answer: True. Elastic scheduling transforms the scheduler’s action space from a binary choice of ‘keep all or kill completely’ to continuous resource adjustment. When higher-priority demand arrives, the scheduler signals the elastic job to shrink worker count down toward \(N_{\text{min}}\), allowing it to continue training at reduced throughput while releasing the remaining nodes for the higher-priority job.
Learning Objective: Compare binary preemption with elastic worker downsizing under sudden cluster contention.
**Order the sequence of events that occurs when a worker node fails during an elastic training run managed by TorchElastic:


The rendezvous backend (e.g., c10d / etcd) detects the dead worker heartbeat and signals a rendezvous state change to remaining workers.
The scheduler detects the unrecoverable node, provisions a replacement node (or authorizes running with reduced workers if within \([N_{\text{min}}, N_{\text{max}}]\)), and joins the new worker.
Active workers pause gradient computation at the step boundary and enter the rendezvous barrier.
All surviving and new worker ranks establish a new communication world, assign new ranks (\(0 \dots N-1\)), re-initialize process groups, load the latest checkpoint, and resume training.
A hardware fault causes an unhandled CUDA kernel crash on worker rank 3, stopping its heartbeats.**

Answer: The correct order is (5) -> (1) -> (3) -> (2) -> (4). Explanation: Step (5): A hardware fault causes an unhandled CUDA kernel crash on worker rank 3, stopping its heartbeats. Step (1): The rendezvous backend (e.g., c10d / etcd) detects the dead worker heartbeat and signals a rendezvous state change to remaining workers. Step (3): Active workers pause gradient computation at the step boundary and enter the rendezvous barrier. Step (2): The scheduler detects the unrecoverable node, provisions a replacement node (or authorizes running with reduced workers if within \([N_{\text{min}}, N_{\text{max}}]\)), and joins the new worker. Step (4): All surviving and new worker ranks establish a new communication world, assign new ranks (\(0 \dots N-1\)), re-initialize process groups, load the latest checkpoint, and resume training.
Learning Objective: Order the operational stages of a dynamic rendezvous event during worker failure and elastic recovery.
← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

When training large foundation models on preemptible/spot cloud GPU instances discounted by \(70\%\) compared to on-demand pricing, what operational vulnerability poses the greatest threat to training goodput?

Spot instances limit maximum GPU memory to half of on-demand instances due to hypervisor virtualization overhead.
Spot preemption events within a single Availability Zone or accelerator pool are often highly correlated during market capacity crunches, simultaneously terminating all nodes in a multi-node gang and causing repetitive re-rendezvous overhead unless checkpoint frequency is tuned.
Spot instances cannot communicate over InfiniBand networks and must route all AllReduce collectives through public HTTP REST APIs.
Cloud providers prohibit running PyTorch or TensorFlow frameworks on spot instances under standard acceptable use policies.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Spot instances offer substantial cost discounts (60-90%) but carry preemption risk. Crucially, spot revocations are not independent random events; during demand surges, cloud providers reclaim entire pools of specific GPU types in a given Availability Zone at once. For multi-node distributed training, losing even a single node halts synchronous training, and frequent correlated preemptions can degrade goodput to zero unless checkpoint intervals and recovery are tightly optimized. Memory limitations, HTTP-only AllReduce, and framework prohibitions are fabricated distractors.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the cost trade-offs and operational risks of running large-scale distributed training on cloud spot instances.
How do Cloud Capacity Blocks (or contiguous reserved GPU instances) differ from standard on-demand and spot instance allocations for large-scale training?

Capacity Blocks guarantee contiguous topological co-location within a single network fabric for a committed time window, eliminating preemption risk and placement fragmentation at the cost of upfront commitment.
Capacity Blocks allow unlimited instantaneous bursting beyond physical cluster limits without financial commitment.
Capacity Blocks dynamically convert idle inference GPUs into spot training nodes with sub-second preemption notices.
Capacity Blocks provide 99% cost discounts by sharing GPU streaming multiprocessors across unrelated cloud tenants.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Capacity reservations / Capacity Blocks allow organizations to reserve contiguous blocks of GPU instances (e.g., hundreds or thousands of H100s connected via high-bandwidth fabrics) for specific project durations (days to months). This guarantees physical co-location and eliminates both the risk of spot preemption and the risk of on-demand capacity unavailability / fragmentation, in exchange for guaranteed utilization commitment. The bursting, dynamic inference conversion, and multi-tenant SM sharing distractors mischaracterize capacity reservation mechanisms.
Learning Objective: Compare capacity reservation mechanisms (such as Cloud Capacity Blocks) with spot and on-demand purchasing models.
Beyond raw accelerator capital expenditure (CapEx) or hourly cloud VM rates, what major operational and infrastructural factors constitute the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) of an ML training cluster?
Answer: Fleet TCO encompasses: (1) Datacenter power and cooling infrastructure (often exceeding \(1-2 \text{ kW}\) per node); (2) High-radix network fabric switches and optical cabling (InfiniBand/RoCE); (3) High-throughput storage arrays and metadata servers for dataset caching and checkpointing; (4) Network egress and cross-AZ data transfer fees; (5) Control-plane management overhead; and (6) Idle capacity costs resulting from scheduling fragmentation and queue wait times.
Learning Objective: Analyze the non-hardware cost factors that contribute to the Total Cost of Ownership of GPU training fleets.
In a distributed training architecture with parameter servers or a central coordinator/master node alongside data-parallel workers, how should roles be partitioned between on-demand and spot instances to optimize cost while maintaining system stability?
Answer: Place the central coordinator/master node, checkpoint metadata store, and primary parameter server on reliable on-demand instances to ensure the control plane never loses state or crashes unexpectedly; allocate elastic, stateless data-parallel workers on discounted spot instances, enabling workers to be preempted and dynamically re-rendezvoused without tearing down the entire training job session.
Learning Objective: Design a fault-tolerant hybrid spot/on-demand placement strategy for distributed training architectures.
True or False: Because each VM instance in a cloud provider has an independent lifecycle, placing worker nodes of a 64-node distributed training job across different instance types within the same Availability Zone guarantees that preemption events will remain uncorrelated and statistically independent.
Answer: False. Cloud capacity pressures and spot revocations are driven by macroeconomic cluster demand spikes and provider-level resource reclamation within a datacenter or Availability Zone. Preemption events for high-demand GPU types (e.g., A100/H100) are heavily correlated within an AZ; when capacity becomes scarce, providers reclaim multiple instances simultaneously, invalidating assumptions of independent failure.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the assumption of statistical independence in cloud spot instance preemption events.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

How does the Tiresias scheduler solve the problem of inaccurate and inflated user runtime estimates in GPU cluster scheduling?

It uses a Two-Dimensional Gittins Index (Least Attained Service) based on observed spatial (GPU count) and temporal (elapsed execution time) resource attainment, prioritizing jobs that have consumed less cumulative compute without asking users for duration estimates.
It requires users to pay monetary deposits that are forfeited if their job runtime deviates by more than \(10\%\) from their initial estimate.
It parses Python ASTs at submission time to statically calculate the exact loop iteration count and FLOP requirements of every training script.
It forces all jobs to run for exactly 60 minutes before automatically killing and requeueing them.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Tiresias eliminates the game-theoretic distortion of user runtime estimates by adopting duration-agnostic scheduling. It implements a 2D Gittins Index (Multi-Level Feedback Queue / Least Attained Service) that tracks both spatial (GPU count) and temporal (time elapsed) resources consumed. Jobs with low attained service are given higher priority, naturally prioritizing short exploratory jobs over long pretraining runs without requiring users to predict runtimes. Financial penalties, AST-based static runtime calculation, and fixed 60-minute time limits are incorrect.
Learning Objective: Explain how Tiresias eliminates reliance on user runtime estimates using Least Attained Service (LAS) scheduling.
In the Pollux scheduling architecture, how is the Goodput** metric (\(G_j\)) defined to co-optimize cluster resource allocation and job-level training dynamics?**

Goodput is the total number of raw GPU clock cycles executed divided by the cluster’s electricity consumption in kilowatt-hours.
Goodput is the ratio of network packets transmitted over InfiniBand to the number of retransmissions caused by packet drops.
Goodput is the product of job training speed (step throughput \(T_j\), steps per second) and statistical efficiency (\(E_j\), progress made per step toward convergence given the current batch size and worker allocation).
Goodput is the percentage of time GPUs spend running CUDA kernels compared to CPU data loading time.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Pollux introduces Goodput \(G_j(a, M) = T_j(a, M) \times E_j(M)\), where \(T_j(a, M)\) is the system throughput (execution speed in steps/second given resource allocation \(a\) and batch size \(M\)) and \(E_j(M)\) is the statistical efficiency (how effectively each gradient step reduces validation loss relative to a baseline batch size). By maximizing total cluster goodput, Pollux dynamically adjusts both resource allocations (GPUs) and training hyperparameters (batch size, learning rate). The other choices define energy efficiency, network reliability, and GPU utilization metrics.
Learning Objective: Apply the Pollux Goodput optimization metric to balance cluster-wide resource allocation and job-level batch size.
What mechanisms does Gandiva use to achieve fine-grained, low-overhead time-slicing and job migration across GPUs?
Answer: Gandiva operates at the granularity of mini-batch iterations. It monitors cyclic execution patterns and executes time-slicing, job suspension, and GPU migration strictly at iteration boundaries when GPU memory contains only model weights (and intermediate activations are deallocated), minimizing memory serialization overhead and eliminating wasted progress between checkpoints.
Learning Objective: Describe the core mechanisms used by Gandiva to achieve low-latency scheduling without wasting training progress.
The custom ML scheduler Themis optimizes for ____ fairness, ensuring that each job completes in a time comparable to what it would achieve in a dedicated cluster share, thereby preventing gaming and multi-resource allocation monopolies.
Answer: finish-time (or finish-time fairness, finish time). Themis designs an auction-based, finish-time fairness metric that balances resource allocation based on how much a scheduler’s decision affects the actual completion time of competing jobs.
Learning Objective: Identify the fairness concept implemented by Themis to prevent users from gaming cluster resource allocators.
**Order these custom ML scheduler milestones chronologically by their introduction of specialized ML scheduling primitives:


Pollux: Co-optimizing cluster resource allocation with dynamic batch size tuning via statistical Goodput modeling.
Gandiva: Iteration-aware scheduling enabling sub-second time-slicing and migration at mini-batch boundaries.
Traditional HPC schedulers (Slurm / PBS): Static batch queue allocation with priority and fair-share decay.
Tiresias: Duration-agnostic 2D Least Attained Service (LAS) scheduling eliminating reliance on user runtime estimates.**

Answer: The correct order is (3) -> (2) -> (4) -> (1). Explanation: Step (3): Traditional HPC schedulers (Slurm / PBS): Static batch queue allocation with priority and fair-share decay. Step (2): Gandiva (OSDI 2018): Iteration-aware scheduling enabling sub-second time-slicing and migration at mini-batch boundaries. Step (4): Tiresias (NSDI 2019): Duration-agnostic 2D Least Attained Service (LAS) scheduling eliminating reliance on user runtime estimates. Step (1): Pollux (OSDI 2021): Co-optimizing cluster resource allocation with dynamic batch size tuning via statistical Goodput modeling.
Learning Objective: Classify and sequence the primary design innovations introduced by research ML schedulers into modern orchestration.
← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why is standard CPU/GPU utilization (such as reported by Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) an ineffective metric for autoscaling LLM inference replicas, and what metric should be used instead?

GPU utilization is strictly proprietary to NVIDIA and cannot be exported to Prometheus.
GPU utilization measures compute core occupancy rather than request latency or queue saturation; an LLM serving replica can be stalled on KV-cache memory capacity or request concurrency while reporting modest GPU SM utilization, making request concurrency or queue depth the superior scaling metric.
GPU utilization fluctuates faster than the speed of light, violating Nyquist sampling criteria in etcd.
LLM serving replicas do not use GPUs during inference, relying entirely on CPU vector instructions.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Standard GPU utilization metrics (SM activity) poorly reflect LLM serving load because models frequently become memory-bound (KV-cache exhaustion) or queue-bound (incoming requests waiting for iteration slots in continuous batching) while SM utilization remains moderate or spiky. Using request concurrency, pending queue depth (e.g., from vLLM/TGI), or TTFT/ITL latency metrics provides a direct, responsive signal for autoscaling. The proprietary claim, Nyquist violation, and CPU-only claim are fictitious distractors.
Learning Objective: Evaluate autoscaling metrics and cold-start latency challenges in LLM serving infrastructure.
In a multi-tenant inference environment hosting multiple smaller models on shared GPUs, what is the primary architectural trade-off between NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) and Multi-Instance GPU (MIG)?

MIG is only supported on consumer GeForce cards, whereas MPS requires enterprise Grace Hopper superchips.
MPS provides sub-nanosecond hardware memory encryption, whereas MIG only supports unencrypted cleartext transfers.
MPS requires dedicated physical PCIe switches per tenant, whereas MIG operates over standard Ethernet cables.
MPS dynamically shares streaming multiprocessors (SMs) and memory bandwidth with high packing density but lacks hard memory fault isolation (an OOM in one client can crash the MPS server), whereas MIG enforces strict hardware isolation (dedicated SMs, memory controllers, L2 cache slices) with full fault isolation but static partition boundaries.

Answer: The correct answer is D. MPS allows multiple processes to concurrently share GPU compute resources (SMs) and memory bandwidth with low kernel launch latency and high utilization, but a memory fault (such as an unhandled CUDA error or OOM) in one process can bring down the entire shared MPS context. MIG provides strict hardware partitioning (dedicated SMs, memory controllers, L2 cache slices) preventing fault propagation and noisy-neighbor effects, but requires static partition profiles that cannot dynamically adapt to shifting request sizes without draining. The other options present incorrect hardware and feature claims.
Learning Objective: Compare GPU resource sharing mechanisms (MIG, MPS, Time-slicing) along isolation, memory protection, and efficiency dimensions.
How can an organization exploit the diurnal traffic cycle of online serving to improve overall GPU fleet utilization, and what preemption mechanism is necessary to protect serving SLOs?
Answer: Online inference demand follows predictable diurnal curves (peaking during business hours and dropping by \(50-70\%\) at night). Organizations can run opportunistic batch training, fine-tuning, or offline evaluation jobs on idle serving GPUs during off-peak hours. To protect latency SLOs during sudden morning traffic surges, the orchestrator must enforce priority preemption with rapid checkpointing or elastic downsizing so training jobs immediately yield capacity back to serving deployments.
Learning Objective: Design an operational policy for harvesting diurnal idle inference GPU capacity for batch training.
Why does reactive autoscaling alone often fail to maintain P99 latency SLOs during sudden inference traffic spikes, and how does predictive autoscaling mitigate this?
Answer: Reactive autoscaling triggers only after metrics (e.g., request queue depth) exceed thresholds, after which provisioning a new GPU container entails pulling multi-gigabyte container images, loading tens of gigabytes of model weights into HBM, and warming up CUDA kernels (a cold start of 30-120 seconds). During this lag, incoming traffic overflows buffers and violates latency SLOs. Predictive autoscaling uses time-series forecasting to pre-provision GPU replicas in advance of anticipated traffic ramps.
Learning Objective: Analyze why predictive autoscaling is necessary to prevent SLO violations during inference traffic spikes.
True or False: In a multi-replica LLM inference cluster, routing user requests randomly via round-robin DNS achieves the highest overall cluster throughput because it balances raw request counts evenly across GPUs.
Answer: False. LLM inference performance depends heavily on KV-cache reuse. Routing requests with shared system prompts or document contexts to the specific GPU replicas that already host the cached prefix in memory (prefix-aware / KV-cache-aware routing) drastically reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) and eliminates redundant prefill compute, outperforming naive round-robin routing.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the interaction between intelligent request routing and GPU memory locality in LLM inference fleets.
In LLM inference serving, while ____ measures the responsiveness before the first output token appears, Inter-Token Latency (ITL) measures the generation speed of subsequent tokens.
Answer: Time to First Token (or TTFT, Time-To-First-Token). TTFT captures prompt processing / prefill latency, which along with ITL defines the end-to-end user experience and service level objectives.
Learning Objective: Identify key performance indicators used in LLM serving autoscaling.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A cluster monitoring dashboard reports \(85\%\) GPU utilization, yet researchers complain of slow progress and low experiment output. What distinction between fleet utilization metrics explains this apparent contradiction?

Allocated utilization (GPUs reserved by containers) may be high (\(85\%\)) while compute utilization (SM active time) is low (\(20\%\)) due to data loader stalls, or productive utilization (goodput advancing converged training steps) is near zero due to unhandled AllReduce synchronization deadlocks.
Hardware sensors on GPUs report utilization in hexadecimal rather than decimal percentages.
Grafana dashboards invert metric percentages when cluster temperature exceeds 25 degrees Celsius.
GPU utilization metrics only count CPU core cycles, concealing whether the GPU is plugged into power.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Cluster observability requires distinguishing between three metrics: (1) Allocated Utilization (fraction of GPUs assigned to jobs, which can be 85%), (2) Compute Utilization (fraction of time GPU SMs are actively executing instructions rather than waiting on CPU data loading, host memory, or I/O), and (3) Productive Utilization / Goodput (fraction of compute advancing valid training steps rather than stalled in communication barriers, deadlocks, or throwaway restarts). The hexadecimal, temperature inversion, and CPU-only options are absurd distractors.
Learning Objective: Differentiate between Allocated Utilization, Compute Utilization, and Productive Goodput in cluster observability.
What is a ‘preemption cascade’ in a multi-tenant GPU cluster, and how can orchestrators mitigate its destructive impact on cluster throughput?

A preemption cascade occurs when a single GPU catches fire and burns adjacent GPUs in the same server rack; it is mitigated by Halon fire suppression systems.
A preemption cascade occurs when Slurm automatically deletes user source code repositories upon job completion; it is mitigated by Git branch protection.
A preemption cascade occurs when Kubernetes continuously restarts healthy pods due to Docker daemon upgrades; it is mitigated by disabling Linux kernel updates.
A preemption cascade occurs when high-priority jobs evict medium-priority jobs, which in turn evict low-priority jobs across the cluster, triggering simultaneous checkpoint I/O storms and thrashing compute progress; it is mitigated by preemption cooldown periods and holistic preemption limits.

Answer: The correct answer is D. In multi-priority environments, an influx of high-priority jobs can evict medium-priority jobs, which then preempt low-priority jobs to find room. If dozens of jobs simultaneously start saving checkpoints before termination, the resulting I/O storm saturates shared storage, prolongs eviction delays, and causes cluster thrashing. Schedulers mitigate this using preemption cooldown timers (preventing a recently started job from immediate re-preemption), holistic bandwidth reservation for checkpointing, and non-preempting priority tiers (preemptionPolicy: Never). The physical fire, code deletion, and Docker upgrade options are incorrect.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the risks of cascading preemption storms and design mechanisms to prevent them.
In a multi-tenant cluster, how does decoupling ‘guaranteed quota’ from ‘limit (burst) quota’ prevent stranded idle capacity while protecting team allocations?
Answer: A guaranteed quota represents a team’s baseline dedicated capacity that is immediately available and immune to eviction by peers. A limit (burst) quota allows a team to opportunistically utilize idle cluster capacity above their guarantee when overall demand is low. If the owning team reclaims their guaranteed quota, the scheduler preempts the bursting team’s opportunistic jobs, maximizing aggregate utilization without violating baseline access rights.
Learning Objective: Explain the architectural difference between guaranteed quota and limit quota in shared GPU clusters.
What is ‘quota hoarding’ in shared GPU clusters, and what automated scheduler policies prevent researchers from engaging in it?
Answer: Quota hoarding occurs when users submit placeholder or dummy sleeping jobs (e.g., interactive shells or infinite loops) to keep GPUs continuously reserved under their quota even when not running useful computation. Schedulers counter this via: (1) Inactivity timeouts that detect zero SM/memory activity and auto-terminate idle sessions; (2) Dynamic lease-based allocations that require active renewal; and (3) Fair-share decay accounting that charges users for holding time regardless of compute intensity.
Learning Objective: Analyze the organizational anti-pattern of quota hoarding and describe governance mechanisms to eliminate it.
True or False: Under Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF), if Team A’s workload requires \(4\text{ GPUs}\) and \(8\text{ CPU cores}\) per worker while Team B’s workload requires \(1\text{ GPU}\) and \(64\text{ CPU cores}\) per worker on a cluster with \(100\text{ GPUs}\) and \(1000\text{ CPU cores}\), DRF equalizes each team’s share of their dominant resource (GPUs for Team A, CPUs for Team B).
Answer: True. Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF) multi-resource allocation identifies each tenant’s dominant resource (the resource type for which the tenant requests the largest fraction of total cluster capacity) and equalizes the dominant shares across all active tenants, ensuring multi-resource equity without allowing single-resource monopolies.
Learning Objective: Apply Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF) principles to multi-resource ML allocations.
**Order the hierarchy of checks performed by a multi-tenant scheduler when Team A in Department X submits a new 16-GPU job request:


Evaluate Team A’s internal user priority and historical fair-share usage decay relative to teammate submissions.
Determine if cluster-wide unallocated capacity or preemption candidates exist to host the 16-GPU allocation.
Verify that Department X has not exceeded its total department-level GPU budget limit.
Check whether Team A’s currently active allocations are within its guaranteed quota or if it must request burst/borrowed capacity.
Grant the lease, bind the containers to physical hardware, and update accounting meters for Department X and Team A.**

Answer: The correct order is (3) -> (4) -> (1) -> (2) -> (5). Explanation: Step (3): Verify that Department X has not exceeded its total department-level GPU budget limit. Step (4): Check whether Team A’s currently active allocations are within its guaranteed quota or if it must request burst/borrowed capacity. Step (1): Evaluate Team A’s internal user priority and historical fair-share usage decay relative to teammate submissions. Step (2): Determine if cluster-wide unallocated capacity or preemption candidates exist to host the 16-GPU allocation. Step (5): Grant the lease, bind the containers to physical hardware, and update accounting meters for Department X and Team A.
Learning Objective: Order the decision hierarchy in a hierarchical multi-tenant fair-share scheduling engine.

Self-Check: Answer

An administrator observes that average GPU compute utilization across a 1,000-GPU cluster is only \(55\%\), yet users experience multi-day queue wait times for 64-GPU jobs. Which diagnostic finding points to the primary root cause?

The cluster’s Ethernet cables are physically too long, causing optical signals to decay into radio waves.
Severe resource fragmentation and strict gang scheduling constraints prevent 64-GPU contiguous blocks from forming, while short jobs hold scattered GPUs across nodes without filling them.
The NVIDIA driver automatically caps utilization at 55% when GPU fans are running on low speed.
Python code running in user containers automatically halts execution whenever cluster utilization drops below 60%.

Answer: The correct answer is B. In multi-tenant GPU clusters, moderate average utilization (e.g., 55%) frequently coexists with long queue times due to fragmentation and gang scheduling requirements: uncoordinated, non-gang small jobs occupy 1-2 GPUs per node across many nodes, leaving hundreds of GPUs idle in aggregate but preventing any single 64-GPU contiguous gang allocation from assembling. Cable length, fan speed capping, and Python auto-halting are fictional distractors.
Learning Objective: Analyze the root causes of high queue wait times coexisting with moderate average cluster utilization.
During a multi-GPU training job, DCGM reports that GPU SM utilization oscillates rapidly between \(10\%\) and \(95\%\) with low memory copy throughput, while top on the host node shows \(100\%\) CPU utilization across all cores and high disk wait (\(iowait\)). What is the root cause and remedy?

The GPU hardware is defective; the operator should replace the GPUs with CPU-only nodes.
The PyTorch model has too many layers; the model architecture must be pruned to 1 layer.
The training job is bottlenecked on host data loading, decompression, or augmentation; the remedy is optimizing PyTorch num_workers, utilizing shared memory (/dev/shm), caching preprocessed tensors on local NVMe SSDs, or offloading transforms to GPU using DALI.
The cluster InfiniBand switch is operating in half-duplex mode; the administrator must power cycle the spine switch.

Answer: The correct answer is C. An oscillating GPU utilization pattern accompanied by pinned host CPU cores and high \(iowait\) is the classic signature of an input data pipeline bottleneck: GPUs finish backpropagation rapidly, then stall waiting for the host CPU DataLoader workers to fetch, decompress, and augment the next batch of training images or tokens. Remedies include increasing/tuning num_workers, storing datasets on local NVMe SSDs, pinning host memory (pin_memory=True), using /dev/shm, or leveraging GPU-accelerated pipelines like NVIDIA DALI. The other options are incorrect diagnoses and destructive actions.
Learning Objective: Identify hardware telemetry patterns indicating host CPU and I/O bottlenecks in GPU training runs.
What is a ‘zombie allocation’ (or ghost job) in a GPU cluster, and how can automated health monitors detect and remediate it?
Answer: A zombie allocation occurs when the scheduler records a GPU as allocated to a running job, but the underlying container or user training process has crashed or entered an unrecoverable CUDA error state, leaving the GPU idle and inaccessible to other users. Automated monitors detect zombies by correlating scheduler allocation tables with DCGM metrics (zero SM and memory activity over a prolonged window) or process tree inspections (no active PID attached to /dev/nvidia*), automatically draining the allocation, killing orphaned processes, and resetting the GPU context.
Learning Objective: Formulate a diagnostic procedure to identify and clean up zombie GPU allocations.
True or False: In a ring AllReduce across 32 nodes, if 31 nodes show \(95\%\) GPU utilization and 1 node shows \(10\%\) utilization, the node with \(10\%\) utilization is the only healthy node while the 31 nodes are encountering network hardware faults.
Answer: False. The reverse is true: in synchronous ring AllReduce, a single slow worker or degraded network link (the straggler) slows down the entire collective; while the straggler takes longer to compute or transfer its chunk, all other 31 workers finish their compute early and spin in the synchronization barrier (often registering high kernel active time in spin-locks or waiting for the straggler to complete). Profiling communication timelines reveals the straggler as the source of the delay.
Learning Objective: Evaluate telemetry signals to pinpoint straggler nodes in multi-node AllReduce rings.
When diagnosing training performance bottlenecks, operators inspect the ____ throughput (measured in GB/s) to ensure that batches transferred from host memory to accelerator HBM are not constrained by host bus contention.
Answer: PCIe (or PCIe bandwidth, PCIe throughput, PCIe transfer). PCIe transfer bandwidth (Host-to-Device / H2D) is a key diagnostic metric for detecting unpinned memory copies and bus saturation during data loading.
Learning Objective: Identify the hardware metric used to diagnose host-to-device data transfer bottlenecks.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why is targeting near \(100\%\) GPU cluster utilization an operational anti-pattern for an interactive AI research and development organization?

GPU hardware components melt if utilization exceeds \(90\%\) for more than 5 consecutive minutes.
Modern deep learning frameworks automatically downgrade model accuracy when cluster utilization exceeds \(85\%\).
Operating above \(95\%\) utilization causes cloud providers to double their hourly billing rates without warning.
As utilization approaches \(100\%\), queuing theory (Pollaczek-Khinchine) dictates that job queue wait times explode hyperbolically, delaying fast feedback for exploratory experiments and severely reducing overall engineering velocity.

Answer: The correct answer is D. According to queuing theory, as cluster utilization (\(\rho\)) approaches \(1.0\), the waiting time in the queue diverges toward infinity (\(W_q \propto \frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\)). In research organizations with heavy-tailed job sizes (\(C_s \approx 3\)), operating above \(80-85\%\) utilization causes small debugging and exploratory jobs to wait days in queues. This destroys developer velocity and feedback loops, proving that maximizing raw utilization at the expense of queue latency is an anti-pattern. Hardware melting, accuracy downgrading, and stealth billing rate doubling are fabricated.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why operating a research GPU cluster at near 100% utilization is counterproductive to organizational velocity.
Explain the fallacy that ‘more sophisticated scheduling algorithms always improve utilization,’ and describe what operators should audit before replacing their cluster scheduler.
Answer: Low cluster utilization and long wait times are more frequently caused by policy misconfigurations than algorithmic limitations. Before replacing or upgrading a scheduler, operators should audit: (1) Resource request inflation (users requesting 8 GPUs when 1 is needed); (2) Unconfigured gang scheduling timeouts; (3) Mismatched hardware partitions (e.g., jobs requiring A100s when A10s suffice); and (4) Stale fair-share decay parameters that fail to balance contention.
Learning Objective: Explain why policy misconfigurations rather than scheduling algorithm limitations are often the root cause of poor cluster efficiency.
True or False: Gang scheduling is strictly mandatory for every distributed ML workload, including asynchronous parameter-server training, hyperparameter sweeps, and elastic fine-tuning jobs.
Answer: False. Gang scheduling is mandatory only for bulk-synchronous parallel training where every worker must reach every AllReduce barrier. Workloads using asynchronous gradient updates (e.g., parameter servers), independent hyperparameter trials, or elastic training frameworks with dynamic worker membership can make useful progress with variable or partial allocations, and enforcing rigid gang scheduling on them unnecessarily increases queue wait times.
Learning Objective: Evaluate when gang scheduling constraints can be relaxed in distributed machine learning workloads.
